3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The 1-IRR is the usual estimator of vaccine efficacy obtained from observed incidence rates in a cohort. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction \(p\) of recipients are completely protected (per-exposure efficacy = 1) while the remainder have zero protection. Early in follow-up the observed incidence-rate ratio therefore equals \(1-p\), correctly recovering the average per-exposure efficacy. Over longer follow-up, however, the pool of susceptible vaccinated individuals is rapidly depleted, so the incidence rate among the vaccinated converges toward the unvaccinated rate. Consequently the time-averaged 1-IRR falls below \(p\), underestimating the per-exposure efficacy parameter of interest. Hence the answer is B.

(The same logic does not apply to a leaky vaccine, where the hazard reduction is constant across all vaccinated persons and 1-IRR recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

The all-or-nothing model means a fraction \(p\) of vaccinated individuals receive complete (sterilizing) protection while the remainder receive none; thus the average per-exposure efficacy equals \(p\). Because the fully susceptible members of the vaccinated cohort are never depleted, their contribution to person-time incidence remains constant. In contrast, the unvaccinated cohort experiences progressive depletion of its most susceptible members, lowering its average incidence rate over time. The net result is that the observed incidence-rate ratio rises toward 1, so that \(1-\text{IRR}<p\). Hence the conventional 1-IRR estimator systematically understates the true per-exposure efficacy. (The bias is absent only in the limiting case of a single exposure or an infinitesimally short follow-up.)

Final answer: B. underestimate

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The 1-IRR will correctly estimate per-exposure VE for an all-or-nothing vaccine. In the standard constant-hazard model, a fraction \(p\) of vaccinees receive complete (sterilizing) protection while the remainder receive none; the observed incidence rate among vaccinees is therefore exactly \((1-p)\) times the rate among controls, so \(1-\text{IRR}=p\), which is also the average per-exposure efficacy. (By contrast, the same estimator is biased for leaky vaccines once susceptibles are depleted.)  
Thus the answer is C.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing (AON) vaccine, a fraction \(\alpha\) of recipients are fully protected and the remainder \(1-\alpha\) receive zero protection. Per-exposure vaccine efficacy is the expected reduction in infection probability on any given exposure; under the AON model this equals exactly \(\alpha\).

Because only the unprotected fraction can become infected, the observed hazard (incidence rate) in the vaccinated arm is precisely \((1-\alpha)\) times the unvaccinated hazard. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio equals \(1-\alpha\) and
\[
1-\text{IRR}=\alpha,
\]
which recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias. (The same numerical value is obtained from a leaky model, but that is irrelevant here; the question asks only whether IRR recovers the AON per-exposure quantity, and it does.)

Thus the correct choice is C.

(The result assumes a constant exposure rate and no waning; both are implicit in the standard definition of per-exposure efficacy.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The key distinction here is between "leaky" vaccines (which reduce infection risk by the same factor for every vaccinated individual on every exposure) versus all-or-nothing vaccines (which confer complete protection to a random fraction \(p\) of vaccinees and zero protection to the rest).  

Under the usual assumption of constant hazards, the observed incidence rate ratio (IRR) directly equals \(1 - \text{VE}_\text{per-exposure}\) only for leaky vaccines. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the hazard ratio is time-varying: initially \(\text{IRR}=1-p\), but as the unprotected vaccinees are depleted the remaining vaccinated cohort becomes progressively enriched for fully protected individuals, so the observed (time-averaged) IRR falls below \(1-p\). Consequently \(1-\text{IRR}\) exceeds \(p\), which means the incidence-rate-based estimator overstates the true per-exposure efficacy parameter.  

Thus the correct choice is A.

(The result is reversed for cumulative-incidence ratios, which underestimate \(p\).)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection in a random fraction \(p\) of recipients, zero protection in the rest). The quantity of interest is therefore the average per-exposure efficacy \(p\).

Under a constant exposure (force of infection) \(\lambda\), the observed incidence rate is cases divided by total person-time. In the unvaccinated arm every participant is susceptible, so person-time is depleted only by infections. In the vaccinated arm the immune fraction contributes “infinite” (or full follow-up) person-time with zero cases. Consequently the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate is inflated relative to the unvaccinated denominator while the numerator is reduced only by the factor \((1-p)\). The resulting incidence-rate ratio is therefore smaller than \(1-p\), which means  
\[
1-\text{IRR} > p.
\]
Hence the 1-IRR overestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. (For short follow-up with negligible depletion the bias vanishes and the estimator is approximately unbiased, but the generic, long-term behavior is overestimation.)

Final answer: A. overestimate

PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of vaccinated individuals are fully protected (hazard 0) while the rest remain fully susceptible (hazard \(\lambda\)), with \(\lambda\) constant for any susceptible individual. The per-exposure vaccine efficacy is exactly \(p\) (complete protection or none).  

Incidence rates are computed over total person-time in each arm. Early in follow-up there is negligible depletion, so IRR \(\approx 1-p\) and \(1-\)IRR recovers \(p\) exactly. Over longer follow-up the unvaccinated arm depletes susceptibles faster than the vaccinated arm; consequently the observed IR in the unvaccinated arm falls relative to the vaccinated arm, the IRR rises toward 1, and \(1-\)IRR falls below \(p\). Thus the 1-incidence-rate-ratio systematically underestimates per-exposure VE.  

The correct choice is therefore B.  

(The same bias does not appear with cumulative incidence ratios, which remain unbiased for \(p\) at any time.)

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction \(p\) of individuals are fully protected (efficacy = 1) while the remainder have zero protection. This \(p\) is exactly the average per-exposure efficacy.  

Under constant exposure, the unvaccinated hazard is constant. In the vaccinated arm, however, the observed population hazard is not constant: it begins at \((1-p)\) times the unvaccinated hazard and monotonically declines toward zero as the unprotected susceptibles are removed, leaving only the permanently immune. Consequently, the total cases per total person-time is lower than \((1-p)\) times the unvaccinated rate. The resulting incidence-rate ratio is therefore biased downward relative to \(1-p\), which means that \(1-\text{IRR}\) exceeds \(p\) and overestimates per-exposure efficacy.  

(The bias vanishes only in the limit of an instantaneous risk period; any appreciable follow-up produces overestimation.)  

Thus the answer is A. overestimate.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The 1-IRR is a standard estimator of VE from cohort data (total cases divided by total person-time at risk). For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fixed fraction \(p\) of recipients are completely protected while the remainder have zero protection. Under a constant external hazard \(\lambda\), the observed average incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is inflated relative to the simple factor \(1-p\) because the unprotected fraction is depleted faster than the unvaccinated cohort; the resulting IRR is therefore smaller than \(1-p\). Consequently 1-IRR > \(p\), which means the estimator overstates the true proportion protected (i.e., overestimates per-exposure VE). Numerical illustration with \(\lambda T=1\), \(p=0.5\) yields IRR \(\approx0.387\) so that 1-IRR \(\approx0.613>0.5\).

Thus the correct choice is A.

For an all-or-nothing vaccine a random fraction \(p\) of recipients are fully protected (hazard 0) while the remainder have hazard \(\lambda\) identical to unvaccinated controls; the quantity of interest is therefore exactly this average per-exposure efficacy \(p\).

Under a constant external force of infection the unvaccinated incidence rate remains \(\lambda\). In the vaccinated arm, however, the protected fraction contributes full follow-up person-time with zero events. This inflates the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate relative to the simple factor \((1-p)\), so the observed IRR falls strictly below \(1-p\). Consequently \(1-\text{IRR}>p\), and the estimator overstates the true per-exposure efficacy. (The bias is zero only in the infinitesimal-follow-up limit; any realistic cohort study produces overestimation.)

This direction of bias is the opposite of the depletion-of-susceptibles effect that appears with cumulative-incidence ratios. The same logic does not apply to leaky vaccines, where the hazard reduction is constant and 1-IRR recovers per-exposure efficacy without bias.

Thus the answer is A.

The incidence rate is cases divided by accumulated person-time at risk (fixed follow-up \(T\), constant external force \(\lambda\)).  

Unvaccinated arm:  
- cases = \(N(1-e^{-\lambda T})\)  
- person-time = \(N(1-e^{-\lambda T})/\lambda\)  
- therefore IR\(_u=\lambda\) exactly.  

All-or-nothing vaccinated arm (\(p\) fully protected):  
- protected fraction contributes \(pNT\) person-time and 0 cases;  
- unprotected fraction behaves exactly like the unvaccinated arm.  
Hence total cases\(_v=(1-p)N(1-e^{-\lambda T})\) while person-time\(_v=pNT+(1-p)N(1-e^{-\lambda T})/\lambda\).  

The extra person-time supplied by the permanently protected individuals therefore makes  
\[
\text{IR}_v<(1-p)\lambda\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\text{IRR}<1-p\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad1-\text{IRR}>p.
\]  
The conventional 1-IRR estimator therefore overstates the true per-exposure efficacy parameter \(p\). (The bias vanishes only for an instantaneous/single-exposure design; any appreciable follow-up produces overestimation.)

The time-averaged IRR therefore lies strictly above \(1-p\), which means \(1-\text{IRR}<p\). The conventional incidence-rate estimator therefore underestimates per-exposure efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine.  

(The direction of bias is the standard depletion-of-susceptibles result and is absent for leaky vaccines.)
